name: Jawline exerciser (Jawzrsize)

lead: Jawline exercisers such as Jawzrsize are handheld devices you bite or chew against with resistance, marketed to strengthen the jaw muscles and give a more defined jawline.

The pitch borrows from muscle-training logic: resistance chewing loads the masseter, which can enlarge with habitual heavy use. No published research on the products or their effect on facial appearance was found.

paras: Users bite into the device in repeated sets as a daily routine, in the same way they would train any other muscle, and compare photos over weeks or months.
Repetitive jaw habits are suggested to be associated with jaw disorders, with limited evidence.

angle.text: Jawline exercisers like Jawzrsize are marketed to users who want stronger, larger jaw muscles and a sharper-looking jawline. You bite against resistance, following muscle-training logic. No studies on the product or its effect on facial appearance exist.

lead: Jawline exercisers such as Jawzrsize are handheld devices, typically a silicone ball or resistance piece that the user bites or chews against, marketed to strengthen the jaw muscles and define the jawline. The idea is that a stronger, larger masseter, the main chewing muscle, adds width and definition at the angle of the jaw, which is the look people are after [1][2]. Jawzrsize was owned and invented by Brandon Harris and, as of a 2018 Healthline report, cost about $30 [2].

Manufacturer claims described by Healthline include a firmer face, a more defined jawline and what the company calls a noninvasive facelift, with resistance of 40+ pounds depending on the model and a suggested 20 to 30 minutes of use daily [2]. Healthline's expert sources said the device works the jaw muscle, and that they were not aware of evidence for the rejuvenation or hair-growth claims [2].

Background research shows the masseter can enlarge with habitual heavy use such as clenching, grinding or constant gum chewing [1]. Controlled studies of jawline exercisers for appearance have not been published. Clinical trials of chewing exercise in older adults have measured bite force and masseter thickness [3][3].
infobox: Jawzrsize, owned and invented by Brandon Harris [2]

paras: Jawzrsize is described by Healthline as a silicone ball that molds to the teeth, which the user bites down on as an exercise. The company's terms state that it makes no medical claims and that use is at the user's own risk [2].

The masseter is among the strongest chewing muscles, and habitual clenching, grinding or constant gum chewing can enlarge it, sometimes unevenly [1]. Jawline exercisers apply the same principle using resistance. Healthline's sources, dental and orofacial pain specialists at the University of Southern California, said the device can build masseter muscle, but that gains are unpredictable, could look bulky, and may be hidden under a fat layer. They said it cannot spot-reduce facial fat or act like Botox [2].

Healthline's experts said that unusual jaw activity can strain the jaw and cause tension headaches, jaw clicking or popping and temporomandibular joint (TMJ) problems, with one noting that a displaced joint disk may be permanent. They also noted chewing without food may cause stomach problems such as acid reflux and gastritis [2].

Jaw habits beyond normal eating and speaking are listed as possible contributors to temporomandibular disorders, with limited evidence, and management guidance favours reversible approaches including gentle jaw exercises as part of physiotherapy [4]. A 2025 systematic review of 8 investigations on chewing gum and temporomandibular disorders reported mixed findings, from no meaningful link to a possible dose-dependent relationship [3].

No studies found on jawline exercisers such as Jawzrsize. Studies of chewing exercise in other settings include a 2026 network meta-analysis in older adults with oral frailty, which found chewing exercise gave the largest bite force gain, though most evidence was rated low to very low certainty [3]. A randomised trial in 50 older adults found biofeedback-assisted masticatory training produced greater gains than gum chewing in occlusal force, masticatory performance and masseter thickness [3].

Forum members debate jawline exercisers within broader lower-third and jawline discussions. Healthline reported that Jawzrsize's online ratings were mostly positive, 3.7 out of 5 on Amazon and 4.4 out of 5 on Facebook, while its expert sources concluded that the claims were not backed by research and that the risks outweighed the benefits [2].

timeline.event: Healthline publishes an expert review of Jawzrsize's claims and risks. [2]
